To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
A forest soil ecosystem harbours a variety of archaeal types, which are associated with specific soil depth layers.

(1) Archaea are ubiquitous among soil microbial community, (2) Archaea community changes along a soil depth profile, (3) Archaea community shifts from the surface to the bottom soil layer, (4) Novel archaeal clusters were found that are associated to either the top or bottom soil layer, and (5) Novel euryarchaeal and crenarchaeotal soil clusters were identified

the archaeal diversity in forest soil ecosystems is much more complex than previously thought, and that archaeal groups are not randomly distributed along the soil depth, but that some groups are associated with specific depth layers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of archaeal groups in soil and with their spatial distribution along a depth gradient.
the identification of novel archaeal groups in soil ecosystems, which are of importance for the understanding of the role and the function of Archaea in soil.
the identification of novel archaeal groups associated with different depth levels of a forest soil and their potential ecological significance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
archaea are not ubiquitous in forest soils, as they are in many soils, but are restricted to specific soil depths.
the distribution of archaeal communities in soil is not random, but rather dependent on the specific environmental conditions of the soil ecosystem.
the archaeal community in the forest soil of Unterehrendinen is highly diverse, and that archaeal diversity is strongly dependent on soil depth.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the archaeal community of the soil is not a homogeneous entity but is rather composed of different archaeal clusters that are distributed along the depth gradient of a forest soil ecosystem.
the soil depth profile is a very important factor in the distribution of archaea.

the archaeal community is not only influenced by the soil type and the soil environment, but also by the soil depth profile and that this influence may be more important than the effect of the soil type.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the archaeal community is highly variable and dynamic in forest soils.
the diversity and distribution of archaeal communities in soils is more complex than previously assumed.
archaeal communities in forest soils can be highly diverse, with different groups dominating at different soil depth layers.
